systems.name: 3DO Interactive Multiplayer
systems.maker: The 3DO Company; built by Panasonic, GoldStar, Sanyo and Creative

units_sold.note: Wikipedia infobox: 2 million units (cited); no as-of date.

systems.summary: A console format from The 3DO Company, started by EA's founder Trip Hawkins and built under licence by Panasonic, GoldStar, Sanyo and others. Its high price kept it behind Sega and Sony.

systems.name: Nintendo 3DS

units_sold.note: Nintendo IR 'Dedicated Video Game Sales Units' page (as of June 30, 2026): Nintendo 3DS hardware 75.94 million, worldwide consolidated, life-to-date (covers the whole 3DS family). Wikipedia infobox lists same figure as units shipped (as of 2022-09-30).

systems.media: 3DS Game Card; SD card for digital
systems.display: Top 3.53" 3D LCD 800x240 (400x240 per eye); bottom 3.00" touch 320x240
systems.summary: The successor to the DS, whose upper screen shows 3D without glasses. The family sold about 75.9 million units before it ended in 2020.

systems.name: Atari 2600

units_sold.note: Wikipedia lead/infobox: estimated 30 million across the system's lifetime (infobox cites a BusinessWeek piece, archived 2007-05-09). No as-of date.

systems.predecessor: Atari Home Pong / Atari Video Pinball
systems.summary: Atari's cartridge console from 1977, which made swappable games a household thing. It stayed in production until 1992.

systems.name: Atari 7800
systems.summary: Atari's successor to the 2600 and 5200, designed by General Computer Corporation. It plays almost all 2600 cartridges, which made it the first console that could run its predecessor's games.

systems.name: Atari Jaguar

units_sold.note: Wikipedia infobox: 250,000 (cited); no as-of date.

systems.cpu: Motorola 68000, 13.295 MHz; two custom RISC processors, 26.591 MHz
systems.media: ROM cartridge; CD-ROM with the Jaguar CD
systems.summary: Atari's last console, sold as the first 64-bit system, a claim others disputed. Its many chips made it hard to program, and 63 licensed games came out.

systems.name: Atari Lynx

units_sold.note: Wikipedia infobox: 2 million (cites a book); no as-of date.

systems.cpu: VLSI VL65NC02 (65C02) in the Mikey chip, 4 MHz
systems.summary: The first handheld with a colour screen, designed at Epyx by two of the Amiga's designers. A smaller Lynx II followed in 1991.

systems.name: ColecoVision

units_sold.note: Wikipedia infobox: more than 2 million (1982–83).

systems.memory: 1 KB RAM, 16 KB video RAM, 8 KB ROM
systems.summary: Coleco's console, closer to the arcades than its rivals, with the first home Donkey Kong in the box. An expansion module plays Atari 2600 cartridges.

systems.name: Dreamcast

units_sold.note: Sega Annual Report 2001 (FY ended Mar 2001): cumulative 8.20 million hardware units since launch (JP, US, Europe, Asia). Wikipedia infobox gives 9.13 million (Routledge), a later cumulative estimate; some sources say 10.6 million.

systems.memory: 16 MB main, 8 MB video, 2 MB sound
systems.summary: Sega's last home console and the first of its generation, with a built-in modem. Sega ended production in 2001 and became a game publisher.

systems.name: Famicom Disk System

units_sold.note: Wikipedia: 4.4 million units when sales of the device ended in 1993.

systems.memory: 32 KB disk cache, 8 KB game RAM
systems.summary: Nintendo's disk drive for the Famicom. Games came on rewritable Disk Cards that shops rewrote with new games for a small fee, and it adds a sound channel.

systems.name: GameCube
aka: ニンテンドーゲームキューブ

units_sold.note: Nintendo lifetime hardware shipments (4.04 M Japan, 12.94 M Americas, 4.77 M other); last increase in FY3/2008, unchanged in the FY3/2016 and FY3/2026 tables

systems.memory: 24 MB main, 3 MB video, 16 MB audio/I/O
systems.media: GameCube Game Disc (8 cm optical disc)
systems.summary: Nintendo's first home console to use optical discs, small 8 cm ones. A compact sixth-generation machine that sold about 21.7 million units.

systems.name: Game Gear

units_sold.note: Approximately 14 million units, as stated in the Wikipedia article

systems.summary: Sega's colour handheld, built on Master System hardware and aimed at the Game Boy. Its backlit screen was a strength, though it used up six AA batteries quickly.

systems.name: Game Boy

units_sold.note: Nintendo reports Game Boy and Game Boy Color together (all variants): 32.47 M Japan, 44.06 M Americas, 42.16 M other. Not a Game Boy-only number; Wikipedia gives 64.42 M for the monochrome models alone in late 1998 (cited to Nintendo data)

systems.display: 2.5 in reflective STN LCD, 160 × 144 px, 4 shades
systems.summary: Nintendo's first handheld with swappable cartridges, designed under Gunpei Yokoi. Simple, tough and frugal with batteries, it ran from 1989 to 2003.

systems.name: Game Boy Advance

units_sold.note: Nintendo lifetime hardware shipments across all GBA models incl. SP and Micro (16.96 M Japan, 41.64 M Americas, 22.91 M other); same 8,151 x 10,000 in the e1603 and e2603 tables

systems.media: Game Pak (also plays GB and GBC Game Paks)
systems.summary: Nintendo's 32-bit handheld, which brought near-SNES graphics to a pocket device. It also plays Game Boy and Game Boy Color games.

systems.name: Game Boy Color
systems.media: Game Boy Color Game Pak (also plays Game Boy Game Pak)
systems.summary: The Game Boy with a colour screen and a faster processor, launched in 1998. It still plays original Game Boy cartridges.

lines.headline: Nintendo · 1998 · fifth generation
lines.sold: 118.7 million, counted with the Game Boy

systems.name: Intellivision

units_sold.note: Wikipedia: more than 3.75 million consoles sold through 1983.

systems.summary: Mattel's console, known for more realistic sports and strategy games than its rivals. INTV Corporation took it over in 1984 and kept it going until 1990.

systems.name: Master System

units_sold.note: Wikipedia infobox/lead: estimated 13 million worldwide (Forster 2005), not counting ~8 million Tectoy variants in Brazil; no as-of date. Sega Retro gives ~20 million (secondary).

systems.summary: Sega's 8-bit console, an export version of the Japanese Mark III. It trailed the NES in Japan and North America but did well in Europe and Brazil.

systems.name: Mega Drive

units_sold.note: Wikipedia: 30.75 million (Sega-produced units, worldwide). Not included: Tectoy ~3M (Brazil), Majesco 1.5M (projected, US). Sega Retro cites ~40M (secondary, interview).

systems.memory: 64 KB RAM, 64 KB VRAM, 8 KB audio RAM
systems.summary: Sega's 16-bit console, sold as the Genesis in North America. Built around a Motorola 68000, it became Sega's best-selling home console.

systems.name: Nintendo 64

units_sold.note: Nintendo lifetime hardware shipments (5.54 M Japan, 20.63 M Americas, 6.75 M other); shipments were effectively zero after FY3/2002, so the total has been stable since then

systems.memory: 4 MB RDRAM (8 MB with Expansion Pak)
systems.summary: Nintendo's last cartridge-based home console and one of the first designed around 3D. Its controller made the analog stick standard for 3D games.

systems.name: Nintendo DS

units_sold.note: Nintendo 'Consolidated Sales Transition by Region' (FY3/2016): Nintendo DS family total 154.02M incl. DS Lite, DSi, DSi XL; Nintendo reports hardware shipments

systems.media: Nintendo DS Game Card (plus Game Boy Advance Game Pak slot)
systems.summary: Nintendo's folding handheld with two screens, the lower one a touchscreen. The DS family sold about 154 million units.

systems.name: Neo Geo CD

units_sold.note: Wikipedia: 570,000 Neo Geo CD units sold worldwide as of 30 September 1997.

systems.summary: The Neo Geo on CD instead of cartridges, so its games cost far less than the AES versions. Loading times of 30 to 60 seconds held it back.

systems.name: Neo Geo AES

units_sold.note: Wikipedia infobox: 410,000 AES home consoles, beside 1 million MVS arcade boards (Game Data Library; Consoles+ no. 73, February 1998).

systems.memory: 64 KB RAM, 84 KB VRAM, 2 KB sound memory
systems.summary: The home version of SNK's MVS arcade board, with the same hardware, so its games play exactly as in the arcade. At first only rented out in Japan, it then sold as a luxury console.

systems.name: Nintendo Entertainment System

units_sold.note: Nintendo lifetime hardware shipments (19.35 M Japan, 34.00 M Americas, 8.56 M other); the NES row has not changed between the FY3/2016 and FY3/2026 tables

systems.memory: 2 KB work RAM, 2 KB video RAM
systems.summary: Nintendo's first cartridge console, launched in Japan as the Famicom in 1983 and brought to North America after the 1983 market crash. It set the template for home consoles and sold about 61.9 million units.

lines.headline: Nintendo · 1983 · third generation
lines.ended_note: 1995 in North America and Europe, 2003 in Japan

systems.name: Neo Geo Pocket Color
systems.cpu: Toshiba TLCS-900/H, 6.144 MHz; Zilog Z80, 3.072 MHz (sound)
systems.memory: 12 KB RAM, 4 KB for the Z80
systems.display: 2.7-inch colour LCD, 160×152, 146 colours on screen out of 4,096
systems.summary: SNK's colour handheld, out a few months after the black-and-white Neo Geo Pocket, whose games it also plays. Liked for its clicky microswitch stick and SNK's fighting games.

systems.name: PC Engine

units_sold.note: Wikipedia infobox: 10 million (HuCard consoles) plus 1.92 million CD-ROM2/Duo units (as of March 1996), i.e. over 11.9 million combined; the body ties the 10 million to Japan as of 1995.

systems.summary: A tiny console by NEC and Hudson Soft that played games on card-sized HuCards. Popular in Japan; it was sold as the TurboGrafx-16 in North America.

systems.name: Pokémon mini
systems.summary: Nintendo's smallest cartridge handheld, made with The Pokémon Company: it fits in a palm and weighs under 70 g. Only ten games came out for it, and a small homebrew scene followed.

systems.name: PlayStation 2

units_sold.as_of: undated (Sony PlayStation history page, fetched 2026-10-22: 'over 160,000,000 consoles sold worldwide since 2000')
units_sold.note: Sony's wording is 'sold'; Wikipedia infobox also 160 million. Guardian 2013-01-04 reported 150 million at end of production.

systems.summary: Sony's second console, which also played DVDs and original PlayStation games. With more than 160 million sold, it is the best-selling home console.

systems.name: PlayStation Portable

units_sold.as_of: undated (Sony PlayStation history page, fetched 2026-10-22: 'Over its lifetime, PSP sold over 80 million units worldwide')
units_sold.note: 'over 80 million'; Wikipedia infobox says 80 million

systems.summary: Sony's first handheld, with a widescreen display and games on UMD discs. It also played video and music and sold over 80 million units.

systems.name: PlayStation

units_sold.as_of: 2005-03-31 (reached; SCEI table shows no change through its last row, 2007-03-31)
units_sold.note: Cumulative production shipments per SCEI, not sell-through

systems.memory: 2 MB RAM, 1 MB video (2 MB in later models)
systems.summary: Sony's first console. Its CD-ROM games helped move the industry from cartridges to discs, and it was the first platform to pass 100 million units shipped.

systems.name: Sega Saturn

units_sold.note: Worldwide total in the Wikipedia infobox; as-of date not stated

systems.memory: 2 MB RAM, 1.5 MB VRAM, 512 KB sound RAM
systems.summary: Sega's CD console with two SH-2 processors, strong in Japan and with arcade-style 2D games. It was followed by the Dreamcast.

systems.name: 32X

units_sold.note: Wikipedia: Sega produced 800,000 32X units and sold an estimated 665,000 by the end of 1994, the rest at steep discounts until 1996.

systems.media: ROM cartridge; CD-ROM with the Sega CD
systems.summary: Sega's add-on that sits in the Mega Drive's cartridge slot and adds two 32-bit SH-2 processors, meant to bridge the gap to the Saturn. It got 40 games of its own.

systems.name: Sega CD

units_sold.note: Wikipedia: 2.24 million Sega CD units sold worldwide when Sega discontinued it in the first quarter of 1996 (Famitsu, 21 June 1996); no as-of date in the article. The article puts the US at 1.5 million and Western Europe at 415,000 by 1994.

systems.memory: 6.5 Mbit RAM, 128 Kbit CD-ROM cache, 64 Kbit backup memory, 1 Mbit boot ROM
systems.summary: Sega's CD-ROM add-on for the Mega Drive, sold as the Mega-CD in Japan and Europe. It has its own 12.5 MHz 68000 and a custom chip for scaling and rotating graphics.

systems.name: SG-1000
systems.summary: Sega's first home console, released in Japan on the same day as Nintendo's Famicom in July 1983. Its line led to the Mark III, sold abroad as the Master System.

systems.name: Super Nintendo Entertainment System

units_sold.note: Nintendo lifetime hardware shipments (17.17 M Japan, 23.35 M Americas, 8.58 M other); identical in the FY3/2015, FY3/2016 and FY3/2026 tables

systems.memory: 128 KB work, 64 KB video, 64 KB audio RAM
systems.summary: Nintendo's 16-bit console, known in Japan as the Super Famicom. Its Mode 7 graphics and sound chip made it a showcase for 2D games through the 1990s.

systems.name: PC Engine SuperGrafx

units_sold.note: Wikipedia: 'selling only 75,000 units total'; no as-of date. Six retail games used its extra hardware.

systems.gpu: 2 × HuC6270 VDC, HuC6202 VPC, HuC6260A VCE
systems.summary: NEC's 1989 follow-up to the PC Engine, rushed out in Japan with a second graphics chip and more memory. Only six games used the extra power, so it sold poorly and was soon left behind.

systems.name: Vectrex
systems.maker: General Consumer Electronics, later Milton Bradley
systems.summary: The only home console with a vector display, on its own built-in screen. Games came with colour overlays for the screen, and Mine Storm is built in.

systems.name: Virtual Boy

units_sold.note: Wikipedia infobox: 770,000 (cited); no as-of date.

systems.memory: 64 KB work RAM, 128 KB graphics DRAM, 128 KB video RAM
systems.summary: Nintendo's tabletop console with a red monochrome 3D display seen through a visor on a stand, made under Gunpei Yokoi. Only 22 games came out before it was dropped in 1996.

systems.name: Wii

units_sold.note: Nintendo lifetime hardware shipments (12.75 M Japan, 48.64 M Americas, 40.23 M other); unchanged at 10,163 x 10,000 since FY3/2016. Wikipedia labels the figure units shipped

systems.media: Wii optical disc (GameCube discs on original model only)
systems.summary: Nintendo's motion-controlled console, which reached far beyond regular players and sold about 101.6 million units. The original model also plays GameCube discs.

systems.name: WonderSwan

units_sold.note: Wikipedia 'estimated 3.5 million' for all models combined (WonderSwan 1.55M, Color at least 1.1M, SwanCrystal roughly 0.85M); secondary sources (Retro Gamer), no Bandai figure found

systems.summary: Bandai's Japan-only handheld, the last hardware Gunpei Yokoi worked on. It could be held upright or sideways and ran on a single AA battery.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WonderSwan (cites Retro Gamer issues 36 and 126, and Koto Laboratory source)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WonderSwan (lead: followed by WonderSwan Color and SwanCrystal)

systems.name: Xbox

units_sold.note: Round figure as Wikipedia gives it; Japan stopped production in 2005, the rest of the world in 2006

systems.summary: Microsoft's first game console, built on PC parts, with a hard drive and Ethernet built in. It launched Xbox Live, and about 24 million were sold.

schema: lines.* are ready-made English display strings (shelf rows); the other fields are the verified data for the details page; sources per system.
